title: Replace a Toilet
summary: Pull out the old toilet, fix the flange if needed, and set a new one on a fresh seal that doesn't rock or leak.
safety: Shut off the water and empty the toilet first. Toilets are heavy and broken porcelain is razor sharp: lift with your legs, wear gloves and get help if needed. Don't overtighten any nut on porcelain. Plug the drain while you work, and remove the plug before you set the new toilet.
pro: the floor around the toilet is soft or rotted, the drain pipe or cast-iron flange is cracked, you want to move the drain, or the shutoff valve won't close. Swapping a toilet in place usually doesn't need a permit, but rules vary: check with your local building department.

questions.label: Wall to bolt center (measured)
questions.hint: Measure from the finished wall, not the baseboard.

questions.label: Flange condition
questions.hint: Not sure yet? Pick Good; you'll check it after the old toilet is out.

calcNote: Rough-in is the distance from the finished wall to the center of the drain (the bolts). If you measure under 9-1/2" or over 15", ask a plumber.

tools.w: The rough-in must match your floor drain. Check that the box includes the tank, bowl and (for two-piece) the tank bolts.
tools.q: {{c.ri}} inch rough in {{a.pieces==='one'?'one piece':'two piece'}} toilet

tools.n: Toilet seat (round or elongated to match)
tools.w: Many toilets come without one.
Seals the toilet to the drain. Never reuse an old one.
tools.qty: 1 (buy 2 in case you have to lift and reset)

tools.w: A foam or rubber seal you can reposition. Check it fits your flange size (3" or 4").

tools.n: Closet bolts with washers, nuts and caps
tools.w: Brass or stainless, so they don't rust in place.

tools.n: Flange repair ring (spanner flange) + stainless screws
tools.w: Screws over a broken flange to give the bolts something solid to hold.
Raises a flange that sits below the finished floor.

tools.n: Braided toilet supply line, 3/8" compression x 7/8" ballcock
tools.w: New is cheap insurance. Check the length (12" or 16" usually) against the old one.
tools.q: toilet supply line 3/8 compression 7/8 ballcock braided

tools.w: Stops a toilet rocking on an uneven floor.

tools.n: Kitchen and bath caulk (white or clear) + caulk gun
tools.w: Seals the base to the floor.
tools.q: kitchen and bath silicone caulk white

tools.w: Closet bolt nuts, tank nuts and the supply line.

tools.n: Stiff putty knife or plastic scraper
tools.w: Scrapes off the old wax.
Measures the rough-in.
Checks the bowl and tank are level.

tools.n: Mini hacksaw or oscillating tool with metal blade
tools.w: Cuts rusted bolts and trims new bolts to length.
Helps rusted nuts come off.
Soak up the water left in the tank and bowl.
Empties the bowl fast and cleanly.

tools.n: Heavy trash bags or cardboard, plus a rag for the drain
tools.w: Somewhere to set the dirty old toilet, and a plug for the drain.
The old wax and drain are dirty.
For cutting bolts and scraping.

steps.idea: The drain's distance from the wall decides which toilets will fit.
steps.b:
1. Find the bolt caps on each side of the old toilet's base.
  2. Hook the tape on the finished wall behind the toilet. If there's a baseboard, hold the tape against the wall above it, not on the baseboard.
  3. Measure straight out to the center of a bolt cap.
  4. Write the number down and enter it above. About 12" means a 12" rough-in toilet; this is by far the most common.
  5. Also measure from the center of the bolt to any side wall or cabinet, and the space in front of the bowl.
faq: I measured 12-1/2". Is that 12?
Yes. Rough-ins are rarely exact. A 12" toilet fits anything from about 12" to 13".
Can I put a 12" toilet on a 10" rough-in?
No, it won't fit against the wall. A 10" toilet on a 12" rough-in fits but leaves a gap behind the tank. Moving the drain is a plumber's job.
How much room do I need around it?
Most US codes want at least 15" from the toilet's center to a side wall or cabinet and 21" of clear space in front. Check local code if your space is tight.

steps.idea: Pick a toilet that fits the rough-in, the room and your local water rules.
steps.b:
1. Buy a toilet with a {{c.ri}}" rough-in. It's printed on the box and spec sheet.
  2. One-piece: tank and bowl are one casting. Easier to clean, heavier (often 80-100 lb), no tank bolts to leak. Two-piece: lighter pieces, cheaper, tank bolts on in 15 minutes.
  3. Elongated bowls stick out about 2" more than round. Check it won't block a door.
  4. Look for 1.28 gallons per flush (WaterSense). Federal law caps new toilets at 1.6 gpf, and some states require 1.28 or less.
  5. Check the box: seat, bolts and wax ring are often sold separately.
  6. Open the box in the store or at home and check the porcelain for cracks before you start.
faq: What's comfort height?
A bowl rim about 17-19" high instead of 15". Easier to sit and stand; standard height is better for kids and shorter people.
Is a 1.28 gpf toilet weaker?
Modern ones flush well. Look up independent flush ratings (MaP scores) if you're worried.

steps.t: Shut off the water and empty the toilet
steps.idea: Get as much water out as you can so the removal is clean and light.
steps.b:
1. Turn the shutoff valve behind the toilet clockwise until it stops. A quarter-turn valve turns 90 degrees until the handle is crosswise to the pipe.
  2. Flush and hold the handle down so the tank drains.
  3. Wait a minute and check the tank: if it refills, the valve isn't closing. Shut off the house main instead.
  4. Sponge or shop-vac the water left in the tank and the bowl into a bucket.
  5. Lay old towels around the base.
steps.stop: If the shutoff valve drips, won't turn, or doesn't stop the water, turn off the main and plan to replace the valve (or call a plumber). Don't force a corroded valve: it can snap off.
faq: Where's the main shutoff?
Usually where the water line enters the house: basement, crawlspace, garage or near the water heater. On a well, turn off the pump at its breaker.

steps.idea: Free the toilet from the water pipe.
steps.b:
1. Hold a small bucket or towel under the tank.
  2. Unscrew the plastic nut under the tank (counterclockwise, as seen from below). It's usually hand-loose.
  3. Leave the line on the valve for now if you'll replace it later, or loosen the nut at the valve with a wrench while you hold the valve body still with a second wrench.

steps.idea: Two nuts hold the toilet to the floor. Rusty ones may need cutting.
steps.b:
1. Pry off the plastic caps on each side of the base.
  2. Turn each nut counterclockwise with the adjustable wrench.
  3. If the bolt spins with the nut, hold the bolt top with pliers while you turn.
  4. Rusted solid? Spray penetrating oil, wait 15 minutes and try again.
  5. Still stuck: cut the bolt between the nut and washer with a mini hacksaw or oscillating tool. Put tape on the porcelain next to the cut.

steps.idea: Break the old wax seal and set the toilet somewhere it can drip.
steps.b:
1. Lay a trash bag or cardboard where you'll set the toilet down.
  2. Two-piece and heavy? Take the tank off first: undo the two nuts under the tank, then lift the tank off. It halves the weight.
  3. Straddle the bowl, grip it at the rim near the tank, bend your knees and keep your back straight.
  4. Rock it gently side to side to break the wax seal, then lift straight up.
  5. Carry it to the bag. Tip it forward a little to drain the water still in the trap.
  6. Stuff a rag into the drain opening right away.
steps.stop: A toilet weighs 60-100 lb and porcelain edges break sharp. Get a helper if you can't lift it comfortably. Cracked porcelain cuts deeply.
faq: It won't budge.
Check for a missed nut or caulk around the base. Cut the caulk with a utility knife, then rock harder.

steps.idea: The new seal needs a clean flange to sit on.
steps.b:
1. With gloves on, scrape the old wax off the flange with the putty knife.
  2. Pull out the old bolts from the flange slots.
  3. Scrape wax off the floor around the flange too, so the new toilet sits flat.
  4. Put the wax in a bag in the trash. Never flush it or wash it down a drain.
  5. Also scrape the wax off the old toilet's outlet if you're giving it away.
faq: Can I scrape with a metal knife on a plastic flange?
Yes, gently. Just don't gouge it.

steps.idea: The flange is what anchors the toilet. It must be solid, round and at the right height.
steps.b:
1. Look for cracks or a broken-off section, especially around the bolt slots.
  2. Push on it: it should be screwed firmly to the floor and not move.
  3. Lay a straightedge across the floor over the flange. The flange top should be on or a little above the finished floor (up to about 1/4" above is fine).
  4. Press around the floor next to the flange with your foot. Soft or spongy floor means rot.
  5. Update your answer about the flange at the top if needed.
steps.stop: Soft, rotted subfloor, a cracked cast-iron pipe, or a flange that isn't attached to anything needs real repair before a toilet goes back on. Call a plumber if you're not sure.
faq: My flange is metal and rusted.
If the ring is rusted through or broken but the pipe is fine, a repair ring screws on top. Rust on a cast-iron pipe itself is a plumber call.

steps.idea: A repair ring screws over the broken part so the bolts have something strong to pull against.
steps.b:
1. Clean the old flange and remove loose broken pieces.
  2. Set the repair ring (spanner flange) on top so its bolt slots line up at 3 and 9 o'clock, parallel to the wall.
  3. Mark the screw holes, drill pilot holes into the subfloor (on concrete you need masonry anchors).
  4. Screw it down with the stainless screws that came with it.
  5. Make sure the ring sits flat and doesn't rock.
faq: Will this raise the flange?
A thin repair ring adds very little. If it lands at floor height or just above, that's right.

steps.idea: A spacer or extender lifts the flange to floor level so the wax compresses properly.
steps.b:
1. Measure how far the flange top is below the finished floor.
  2. Stack spacer rings (or use the extender) to reach floor level or slightly above.
  3. Put the gasket or a bead of silicone between each layer as the kit says.
  4. Screw the spacer to the old flange with the kit's long screws.
  5. Use the longer closet bolts that come with the kit if the stock ones are too short.
faq: Can I just use two wax rings?
Some plumbers do, but stacked rings can slip and leak. A spacer kit is the reliable fix.
What about a wax ring with a horn?
The plastic horn helps guide water, but it doesn't fix a low flange by itself.

steps.idea: Two new bolts, standing straight up, parallel to the wall.
steps.b:
1. Slide each bolt head into the flange slot, head down.
  2. Move them to the 3 and 9 o'clock positions so they're the same distance from the wall.
  3. Snap the plastic washers on to hold them upright.
  4. Measure from the wall to each bolt: both should match.

steps.idea: Test the fit without the seal, so any surprises cost nothing.
steps.b:
1. Take the rag out of the drain for a moment and set the bowl on the bolts without the seal. Have a helper if it's heavy.
  2. Check the bolts come up through the holes in the base.
  3. Push on the corners: does it rock? Note where, and how many shims it takes.
  4. Check the tank or tank holes clear the wall.
  5. Trace the base outline with a pencil, lift the bowl off and put the rag back.
faq: The bolts don't line up with the holes.
Slide them in the slots until they do. If the base hits the wall, your rough-in or toilet doesn't match.

steps.idea: The seal goes between the toilet's outlet and the flange.
steps.b:
1. Lay the bowl on its side on a towel or cardboard.
  2. {{a.seal==='wax'?'Keep the wax ring at room temperature. Peel off the plastic.':'Read the seal\'s instructions: most go on the flange, some on the toilet.'}}
  3. {{a.seal==='wax'?'Press the flat side of the ring onto the outlet horn on the bottom of the toilet. The plastic horn (if any) points down, toward the drain.':'Press the seal on firmly and centered.'}}
  4. Take the rag out of the drain.
  5. Look into the drain once more: it must be empty.
steps.stop: Take the rag out of the drain now. A rag left in the pipe causes a clog you can only fix by pulling the toilet again.
faq: Wax or wax-free?
Wax is the cheap, proven standard. Wax-free seals can be repositioned and are cleaner, but cost more and must match your flange.
Ring on the flange or on the toilet?
Either works. On the toilet is easier to keep centered when you set it down.

steps.idea: Lower the bowl onto the bolts in one move so the seal squashes evenly.
steps.b:
1. Lift the bowl, stand over the flange and look through the bolt holes to line them up.
  2. Lower it straight down onto the bolts. Don't slide or twist it.
  3. Sit on it, or press down on the rim with both hands, and rock gently front to back until the base meets the floor.
  4. Check it lines up with your pencil outline.
steps.stop: If you have to lift the toilet back up after it touched the seal, scrape it off and use a new wax ring. A disturbed ring leaks.
faq: The base won't come down to the floor.
The flange may be too high or the ring too thick. Don't force it with the nuts. Lift, check, and use a standard ring.

steps.idea: A rocking toilet breaks its own seal over time.
steps.b:
1. Push on each corner. It shouldn't move.
  2. If it rocks, slide plastic shims under the low side until it's solid.
  3. Check level side to side on the bowl rim. A slight tilt front to back is fine.
  4. Leave the shim ends sticking out for now. You'll trim them after the caulk.

steps.idea: Pull the bowl down evenly, a little at a time, so the porcelain doesn't crack.
steps.b:
1. Put a washer and nut on each bolt. Thread them on by hand.
  2. Turn the left nut 1/4 turn with the wrench, then the right nut 1/4 turn.
  3. Keep alternating until the toilet doesn't move when you push it.
  4. Stop there. If the nut needs force, you're done.
  5. Cut the bolts off a little above the nut with the mini hacksaw so the caps fit, then snap the caps on.
steps.stop: Overtightening cracks the base, sometimes hours later. Snug is enough.
faq: Can I trim the bolts before tightening?
No. Trim after, so the nut has full threads to pull on.

steps.idea: Two-piece toilets bolt the tank onto the bowl with a rubber gasket between.
steps.b:
1. Turn the tank over on a towel. Push the big rubber gasket over the nut on the bottom.
  2. Put the bolts through the tank from inside with the rubber washers under the bolt heads.
  3. Lower the tank onto the bowl so the bolts drop through the holes.
  4. Thread on the washers and nuts underneath.
  5. Tighten a few turns on one side, then the other. Hold the bolt head inside with a screwdriver while you turn the nut.
  6. Stop when the tank sits level and doesn't wobble. Porcelain should not touch porcelain on most models; follow the instructions.
steps.stop: Don't crank the tank nuts. A cracked tank floods the bathroom.

steps.idea: A new braided line from the valve to the fill valve.
steps.b:
1. Thread the plastic nut onto the fill valve under the tank. Hand-tight, then a quarter turn more.
  2. Thread the other end onto the shutoff valve. Hand-tight, then 1/4 to 1/2 turn with a wrench while a second wrench holds the valve body still.
  3. Check the line curves gently with no kinks.
faq: Do I need thread tape?
No. Both ends seal with a rubber washer or compression cone, not threads.
The old line is short metal tubing.
Replace it with a braided line. It's easier and less likely to leak.

steps.t: Turn on the water and check for leaks
steps.idea: Fill, flush, look and touch: catch leaks now while it's easy to fix.
steps.b:
1. Open the shutoff valve slowly, all the way.
  2. Let the tank fill. Check the water stops at the fill line marked inside the tank.
  3. Wipe all joints dry. Flush 5-10 times.
  4. Run a dry tissue around the supply nuts, tank bolts and the base. Any wet spot is a leak.
  5. Check again after an hour, and the next morning.
faq: Water at the base after flushing.
Stop using it. The seal isn't good: pull the toilet, scrape, and reset with a new ring.
Drip from a tank bolt.
Tighten that bolt's nut 1/8 turn while you hold the bolt head. If it still drips, the washer is misaligned: drain and reseat.

steps.idea: Seal the base to the floor, but leave the back open so a leak can show.
steps.b:
1. Install the seat with its bolts. Hand-tight, they're plastic.
  2. Wipe the floor and base clean and dry.
  3. Run a thin bead of caulk around the front and sides of the base.
  4. Leave a 1-2" gap at the back, centered.
  5. Smooth the bead with a wet finger. Wipe extra away with a damp rag.
  6. After the caulk sets, snap or cut the shims flush with the base.
  7. Keep mop water off the caulk for 24 hours.
faq: Does code require caulking?
Many local codes require the base to be sealed to the floor. The back gap is common practice; if your inspector objects, seal all the way around.
Can I use the toilet right away?
Yes, just don't bump the fresh caulk.

steps.t: Get rid of the old toilet
steps.idea: Old porcelain is heavy, sharp and usually not curbside trash.
steps.b:
1. Drain any water left in it.
  2. Check your city's bulky waste or recycling rules. Many towns take toilets for crushing.
  3. Some stores take the old one back with delivery, so ask when you buy.

evenTighten.b:
1. Thread every nut on by hand first.
  2. Turn one nut a quarter turn with the wrench, then the other.
  3. Keep alternating.
  4. Stop as soon as the part doesn't move when you push it.
  5. Never lean on the wrench. Porcelain cracks without warning.

cutBolt.b:
1. Put on safety glasses.
  2. Spray penetrating oil and wait 15 minutes. Try the nut once more.
  3. Put masking tape on the porcelain next to the nut.
  4. Cut through the bolt just below the nut with a mini hacksaw or an oscillating tool with a metal blade.
  5. Let the tool do the work; don't twist the blade against the porcelain.

leakCheck.b:
1. Wipe every joint completely dry.
  2. Run water or flush a few times.
  3. Touch each joint with a dry tissue or paper towel. Any wet mark is a leak.
  4. Check again after an hour and the next day: slow leaks take time to show.

setdown.title: Set the toilet
setdown.cap: Lower the bowl straight onto the bolts in one move, then press down on the seat with your body weight and rock gently to squash the wax.

alternate.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Tighten a little, side to side</text><rect x="90" y="34" width="140" height="112" rx="40" class="tb"/><circle cx="110" cy="90" r="7" class="bk"/><circle cx="110" cy="90" r="2.5" class="inkf"/><circle cx="210" cy="90" r="7" class="bk"/><circle cx="210" cy="90" r="2.5" class="inkf"/><circle cx="110" cy="66" r="8" class="af"/><text x="110" y="69" class="nm" text-anchor="middle">1</text><circle cx="210" cy="66" r="8" class="af"/><text x="210" y="69" class="nm" text-anchor="middle">2</text><path d="M122 56 Q160 34 198 56" class="a" fill="none"/><polygon points="198.0,56.0 192.1,56.9 193.6,51.9" class="af"/><text x="122" y="114" text-anchor="middle">1/4 turn</text><text x="198" y="114" text-anchor="middle">1/4 turn</text><text x="10" y="166">Repeat until snug and the toilet doesn't move.</text><text x="10" y="179" class="wa">Too tight cracks the porcelain.</text>
alternate.cap: Snug means the base is tight to the floor and doesn't shift when you push it. It does not mean as tight as you can go.

shim.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Rocks? Shim it, then tighten</text><path d="M10 118 L310 108 L310 124 L10 134 Z" class="tl"/><path d="M84 60 H240 L236 110 H84 Z" class="tb"/><path d="M52 116.3 L96 110 L96 114.8 Z" class="y"/><text x="24" y="98" class="ac">shim</text><line x1="40" y1="100" x2="62" y2="112" class="a"/><text x="160" y="90" text-anchor="middle">toilet base</text><text x="10" y="152">Slide plastic shims into the gap until solid.</text><text x="10" y="165">Snap off the extra after caulking.</text>
shim.cap: Use plastic toilet shims, not wood (wood rots). Shim where the base lifts when you rock it, then tighten the nuts again.

caulk.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Caulk the base, leave the back open</text><rect x="20" y="26" width="280" height="8" class="b"/><text x="24" y="50">wall</text><rect x="100" y="56" width="120" height="110" rx="40" class="tb"/><path d="M140 53 A43 43 0 0 0 97 96 V126 A43 43 0 0 0 140 169 H180 A43 43 0 0 0 223 126 V96 A43 43 0 0 0 180 53" class="a" fill="none" style="stroke-width:3"/><text x="160" y="48" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">leave 1-2" open</text><text x="232" y="110" class="ac">caulk bead</text><text x="10" y="186">A leak then shows on the floor instead of hiding.</text>
caulk.cap: Caulk keeps mop water out and stops the base from shifting. The open gap at the back lets a future wax-ring leak show up early.

supply.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Connect the new supply line</text><rect x="20" y="24" width="8" height="140" class="b"/><rect x="150" y="30" width="120" height="70" rx="4" class="tb"/><text x="210" y="66" text-anchor="middle">tank</text><rect x="196" y="100" width="12" height="14" class="bk"/><rect x="190" y="110" width="24" height="10" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="28" y="142" width="20" height="10" class="bk"/><rect x="48" y="134" width="20" height="24" rx="3" class="bk"/><rect x="68" y="141" width="14" height="10" rx="2" class="y"/><rect x="51" y="122" width="14" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><path d="M58 122 C58 60 202 150 202 120" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:5"/><path d="M58 122 C58 60 202 150 202 120" class="th-l d" fill="none" style="stroke-width:1"/><text x="222" y="124" class="k">hand-tight</text><text x="222" y="136">+ 1/4 turn</text><text x="90" y="154" class="k">compression nut</text><text x="90" y="166">snug + 1/4 to 1/2 turn</text><text x="10" y="190">No thread tape here: the seals do the work.</text>
supply.cap: Most toilets need a 3/8" compression x 7/8" ballcock braided line. Buy one a few inches longer than the gap so it can curve gently, with no kinks.

tank.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Two-piece: tank onto the bowl</text><rect x="60" y="30" width="200" height="50" rx="3" class="tb"/><text x="160" y="58" text-anchor="middle">tank</text><rect x="140" y="80" width="40" height="8" class="bk"/><rect x="128" y="84" width="64" height="20" rx="4" class="mp"/><text x="160" y="97" text-anchor="middle">gasket</text><rect x="50" y="104" width="220" height="40" rx="3" class="tb"/><text x="160" y="128" text-anchor="middle">bowl</text><line x1="90" y1="66" x2="90" y2="158" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="82" y="72" width="16" height="6" class="inkf"/><rect x="84" y="66" width="12" height="6" class="bk"/><rect x="82" y="144" width="16" height="4" class="bk"/><rect x="84" y="148" width="12" height="8" class="inkf"/><line x1="230" y1="66" x2="230" y2="158" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="222" y="72" width="16" height="6" class="inkf"/><rect x="224" y="66" width="12" height="6" class="bk"/><rect x="222" y="144" width="16" height="4" class="bk"/><rect x="224" y="148" width="12" height="8" class="inkf"/><text x="10" y="62">rubber</text><text x="10" y="73">washer</text><text x="10" y="84">inside</text><text x="244" y="160">washer + nut</text><text x="10" y="174">Tighten side to side until the tank is level</text><text x="10" y="186">and doesn't wobble. Then stop.</text>
tank.cap: The rubber washers go inside the tank, under the bolt heads: they are what keeps the water in. Porcelain cracks if you crank the nuts.

cutbolt.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Stuck nut? Cut the bolt</text><rect x="10" y="130" width="300" height="8" class="tl"/><rect x="60" y="90" width="200" height="40" rx="3" class="tb"/><line x1="160" y1="58" x2="160" y2="130" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="146" y="84" width="28" height="6" class="bk"/><rect x="150" y="70" width="20" height="12" class="inkf"/><line x1="136" y1="83" x2="184" y2="83" class="a d"/><rect x="190" y="78" width="110" height="6" rx="1" class="y"/><path d="M190 84 l3 4 l3 -4 l3 4 l3 -4 l3 4 l3 -4 l3 4 l3 -4 l3 4 l3 -4 l3 4 l3 -4" class="o" fill="none" style="stroke-width:1"/><text x="196" y="68" class="k">oscillating blade</text><text x="10" y="66">cut between</text><text x="10" y="77">nut and washer</text><line x1="88" y1="76" x2="134" y2="83" class="o"/><text x="10" y="152">Wear glasses. Tape guards the porcelain.</text>
cutbolt.cap: Spray penetrating oil first and wait 15 minutes. If the nut still spins the bolt, cut through the bolt just above the washer.

glossary: Distance from the finished wall to the center of the toilet drain. 12" is standard.
The round fitting on top of the drain pipe that the toilet bolts to. Also called a closet flange.
The two bolts that stick up from the flange and hold the toilet down.
A ring of wax that seals the toilet outlet to the flange.
The flexible hose from the shutoff valve to the toilet.
The small valve on the wall or floor behind the toilet. Also called an angle stop.
The valve inside the tank that refills it after a flush.
A thin plastic wedge that fills a gap under the base.
